## Abstract

Data-driven dynamical models are increasingly fitted to walking, yet gait dynamics are still most often summarized by asymptotic stability, which says whether a disturbance eventually dies out but little about how walking responds in the meantime. Recordings of walking are dominated by the average stride, which describes walking when nothing happens; how walking responds to disturbances and recovers lies in the departures from it, and only a model of the dynamics can predict and explain them. The size and duration of a disturbance, the movements that compensate for it, and the course of recovery can differ even when long-term stability is similar. Non-normal dynamics can amplify disturbances before they decay, while active control and repeated forcing shape the response observed during walking. Floquet multipliers summarize only part of that behavior and are difficult to estimate reliably from short, noisy recordings. We argue for models that describe the evolving gait dynamics and predict meaningful departures from ordinary walking. We identify six requirements: useful response predictions, credible sustained behavior, reproducibility, practical performance with realistic recordings, interpretable dynamical structure, and comparability across people and conditions. Comparisons on oscillators, a walking template, and human gait support linear models in delay coordinates as a strong practical foundation across these requirements. Nonlinear models can predict particular recoveries more accurately; the case for linear models rests on their combined strengths and the tools available to examine their responses. Appropriate perturbation data and independent validation remain essential. A model that reproduces the gait cycle has not yet demonstrated that it captures how walking responds and recovers.

## What do we need to understand about walking?

Walking is a rhythm produced by interacting body mechanics, neural control, and the environment, and it is disturbed and corrected at every stride. Each foot's collision with the ground, uneven terrain, the body itself, and the variability of neural control push it off its usual course, and it returns within a stride or two (@fig-transient). A recording of walking is therefore a repeating cycle plus departures from it (@fig-overview A). The average stride describes most of the recording: in treadmill trials of 15 s from 42 people, about 98% of the joint angles' variance (@fig-gait-mean). It describes what walking does when nothing happens. The departures are the responses to disturbances. They are small, but they spread over many more directions of movement than the cycle: over the last quarter of a stride of six joint angles, ten principal directions carry 90% of their variance, against four for the whole signal.

Why model the dynamics rather than describe the average stride? The questions that matter for falls, rehabilitation, assistive devices, and individual differences in control concern what happens when something does happen: how large a departure becomes after a disturbance, how long it lasts, which joints and limbs carry it, whether its effect depends on when in the stride it arrives, and whether it shifts the timing of the gait. The average stride answers none of these, because it says nothing about how the present state of the body determines its future. Two systems can share the same cycle, and so the same average stride, yet respond to the same push in entirely different ways (@fig-overview B). A dynamical model describes exactly that dependence: from where the body is now, including its departure from the average stride, it predicts where the body will be next. It can therefore forecast responses, run forward on its own, and expose the structure that produces them. The same reasoning sets the test such a model must pass. A model that reproduces the average stride, or forecasts the recorded signal closely because the recording is mostly the average stride, has not shown that it captures the dynamics; it must forecast the departures better than the average stride does. Throughout, we score forecasts by the variance of the departures they leave, relative to the variance left by forecasting the average stride (relative remaining variance; 1 is no better than the average stride, 0 an exact forecast).

Three traditions describe this behaviour. Mechanistic templates and musculoskeletal simulations represent the interactions explicitly, but fitting them to individuals and predicting changes in kinematics remain difficult [@winner2023]. Stability and variability measures offer compact descriptions computed from movement recordings [@dingwell2000; @dingwell2006; @bruijn2013]. Each reads one part of the response to a disturbance (@fig-overview C): a short-term Lyapunov exponent its early rate of divergence, a Floquet multiplier its late rate of return. Neither describes how large the response becomes, when, or which movements carry it, and two systems that share both numbers can respond differently. The margin of stability evaluates the state at a single instant relative to the base of support [@hof2005] and so describes no response at all. Data-driven dynamical models provide another route: learning how observed movements evolve, from linear step-to-step maps to nonlinear sequence models [@revzen2012; @winner2023].

The value of such a model lies in the questions it can answer about the response. We identify six requirements for it (@fig-overview D): forecasting the response (R1), credible sustained behaviour (R2), reproducible answers (R3), practicality with realistic recordings (R4), interpretable dynamical structure (R5), and comparability across people and conditions (R6). We first explain why asymptotic stability is an inadequate primary target, both conceptually and in its practical estimation. We then define the requirements and compare modeling approaches against them on oscillators, a walking model, and human walking and running. Linear models offer a particularly useful combination of reproducibility, tractability, and accessible dynamical analysis; their promise is a broader description of walking and recovery, with predictions and interpretations that can be tested.

![**Why model the dynamics of walking, and what such a model must provide.** Schematic. (A) A recording of walking is a repeating average stride plus departures from it, the responses to the disturbances that walking meets at every step (@fig-transient). The average stride is what walking does when nothing happens; the departures are small, a few percent of the variance in the gait recordings of @fig-gait-mean, but spread over many directions of movement. Two systems with the same cycle, traversed at the same rate and therefore with the same average stride, respond differently to the same push: one returns within half a stride, the other over several strides (exact solutions of two planar oscillators). ## Why asymptotic stability is not the right primary target

### A long-term return rate does not describe the recovery that matters

Floquet multipliers characterize whether sufficiently small deviations from a periodic orbit eventually shrink and their asymptotic rates of change per cycle. This makes them a natural measure of local gait stability [@dingwell2006], but leaves much of the recovery unspecified.

Walking never settles into the regime that a multiplier describes (@fig-transient). A multiplier gives the rate at which a deviation shrinks once only its slowest component remains, and reaching that regime takes several strides: at the multipliers reported for human walking, about 0.3–0.8 per stride [@dingwell2006; @bruijn2013], a single disturbance needs roughly 2–10 strides to fall to a tenth of its size. Walking is disturbed far more often. Each step's collision with the ground redirects the body's motion [@kuo2005], foot placement is adjusted from step to step [@wang2014; @bruijn2018], and terrain, the body, and neural control add variability throughout the stride. The deviation observed at any moment is therefore a superposition of responses to recent disturbances, most still within their first stride or two. Stride-to-stride variability is a property of these short-time responses rather than of their eventual rate, and the response over the first strides after a disturbance is the behaviour a model must capture.

![**Walking is disturbed again before it recovers, and its short-time response is not what the multiplier predicts.** Ground truth, no fitting; norms in observed coordinates (each variable scaled by its SD along the cycle). (C) Stride to stride: worst-case growth of the n-stride map from the cycle against the multiplier's prediction ρⁿ (dashed), for coupled FHN and SLIP with feedback (two steps per stride). (D) Share of the observed deviation (stationary variance) contributed by disturbances younger than a given age. Coupled FHN with continuous disturbances of equal size in every variable, one cycle taken as one stride; SLIP with one disturbance per step, with speed feedback and open loop (ρ = 0.95 per step); grey band, a one-dimensional stride map with the multipliers reported for human walking, 1 − ρ^2n^. Shading in B–D, the first cycle or stride. The oscillator family behind B and lasting phase shifts are in @suppfig-oscillators.](figures/Figure_02){#fig-transient fig-alt="Four panels: a SLIP walker's centre-of-mass height with a disturbance at every step and its deviation as the sum of overlapping responses; one disturbance's distance from the cycle in coupled FHN against the multiplier's prediction, within a stride and from stride to stride; and the share of the observed deviation contributed by disturbances younger than a given age."}

A disturbance can grow before it decays. In a non-normal system, interactions between response directions can produce transient amplification even when all transverse multipliers indicate eventual return [@trefethen2005; @hess2026nonnormality]. The direction and phase of the disturbance affect its peak size, its redistribution between movements, and the time course of recovery. The ground-truth examples show growth that the multiplier misses, both within a stride and from one stride to the next (@fig-transient B–C); it appears across a family of oscillators with very different multipliers (@suppfig-oscillators).


Because the observed deviations are responses to ongoing disturbances under active control, they reflect forcing, mechanics, and feedback together. Beyond a local linear approximation, overlapping responses can also interact nonlinearly. An estimated multiplier describes aspects of the combined system and does not separately identify the mechanical plant or neural controller.

Persistent changes in timing and coordination provide further reasons to examine the trajectory. A phase shift can leave a person walking on the same cycle at a different time (@suppfig-oscillators C), while a coordination disturbance changes the relation between movements. Both can matter even when motion remains bounded. The full response is therefore the object of interest; its asymptotic rate is one summary.

### Even the stability number is difficult to recover from gait data

The practical problem compounds the conceptual one. Short recordings contain relatively few independent strides despite many within-stride samples. Measurement noise, the chosen state variables and gait event, and approximation of the dynamics all affect an estimated return map.

The SLIP walking example makes these difficulties concrete (@fig-floquet-maps). More strides reduce scatter without necessarily removing measurement-noise bias. Phase-indexed and piecewise-linear models provide more detailed descriptions within the cycle, but their composed return maps remain sensitive to noise and the partition used. Dividing a stride into more pieces does not by itself resolve the estimation problem.

![**Data-driven Floquet multipliers of SLIP walking are data-hungry and biased by measurement noise; for a linear map the bias is correctable.** Kicked SLIP walks (stride-level kicks at vertical leg orientation, VLO; open loop, truth 0.628 ± 0.713i, ρ = 0.95), 20 walks of 2000 steps; measurement noise is relative to the stride-to-stride SD of each variable. (A) Eigenvalues of the VLO return map from 20 walks: 30 steps with noise 0.25×, and 2000 noise-free steps; star, truth; dotted, unit circle. (B) Estimated spectral radius against record length, noise-free (solid) and with noise 0.25× (dashed); median and interquartile range over walks. More strides reduce the scatter, not the bias; the section map by instrumental variables (IV; previous step as the instrument) removes it. (C) Against measurement noise, 250 steps: section map by least squares and by IV, phase-indexed maps, and 8-sector piecewise-linear maps. (D) Piecewise-linear maps against the number of sectors composed over one step, 250 steps.](figures/Figure_03){#fig-floquet-maps fig-alt="Four panels: return-map eigenvalues in the complex plane, estimated spectral radius against record length, against measurement noise, and against the number of piecewise sectors."}

The instrumental-variable correction is a constructive result: under the tested assumptions, linear-map estimation allows a substantial noise bias to be corrected [@dawson2016; @hemati2017; @askham2018]. It does not make the multiplier a complete description of recovery. Together, the conceptual and estimation challenges motivate models that can answer richer questions about the evolving response.

## What should a useful model of gait dynamics provide?

Replacing one stability estimate with a more complicated model helps only if the model answers questions the estimate cannot. We want a model of the gait pattern and the evolution of departures from it: disturbances, compensatory coordination, and recovery considered together. This does not require claiming to reconstruct every physiological mechanism from kinematics.

### The capabilities that matter

The six requirements of @fig-overview D are:

1. **Forecast the response to disturbances (R1).** From an observed state, predict how the deviation from the usual cycle evolves over the following strides, including its size, direction, timing, and return, more accurately than reference forecasts such as the mean cycle. This applies to ordinary walking, whose deviations are themselves responses to ongoing disturbances (@fig-transient), and to larger disturbances of the kinds represented in the training data. Assess timing errors separately from errors in amplitude and coordination.
2. **Remain credible beyond a short fitted segment (R2).** Produce plausible sustained walking and bounded trajectories over the intended observation window. A good short fit alone is insufficient.
3. **Give reproducible answers (R3).** Conclusions about a person or condition should not depend strongly on arbitrary fitting initializations.
4. **Work with realistic recordings (R4).** Establish sensitivity to noise, record length, partial observation, and available excitation, and make uncertainty and data requirements visible. A model that works on real data must also be practical to fit and validate on it, without prohibitive computation or opaque tuning.
5. **Expose interpretable dynamical structure (R5).** Allow examination of how disturbances spread between movements, where amplification occurs, and which responses dominate.
6. **Support comparison across people and conditions (R6).** Fitted models should share a structure in which the same quantities can be computed and compared between participants, conditions, and tasks, so that differences reflect the dynamics rather than the fit.

### What data are needed to meet those requirements?

Repeated similar strides can describe the usual gait pattern well while revealing little about responses to substantial disturbances. Systems can share a periodic orbit yet differ away from it. Passive recordings may contain informative deviations, but their adequacy must be demonstrated for the particular response being claimed.

Human gait recordings show the problem directly. In 299 treadmill trials of 15 s, most of each trial's variance lies in the mean cycle, and the deviations that carry the response to disturbances are a small remainder (@fig-gait-mean A–B). Whole-trajectory operator measures can inherit that structure: much of the companion paper's transient-growth signature at a one-third-stride window is reproduced by the mean cycle alone (@fig-gait-mean C–D). This does not make the waveform unimportant; it limits what such a signature alone establishes about recovery, and it means a model can fit a recording closely while learning little about its deviations.

(A) One able-bodied trial (14 strides at 124 cm/s): knee angle of every stride (grey) and the mean cycle (black); below, each stride's deviation from the mean cycle. (B) Share of each trial's variance in the deviations against the number of strides in the trial. (C) Transient growth (TG) of the companion paper's operator [@hess2026nonnormality] (delay DMD, rank 70, ridge 10^−4^, stride-rescaled time; TG = max over one stride of ‖Ãᵏ‖) against the delay window: recorded trials (solid) and each trial's mean cycle repeated with no deviations (dashed); medians. (D) What the deviations add: per-trial Δlog₁₀ TG, recorded minus mean cycle only; median and interquartile range.](figures/Figure_04){#fig-gait-mean fig-alt="One gait trial's strides and deviations, deviation share of variance against strides per trial, transient growth against delay window for recorded trials and mean cycle only, and the increase due to deviations."}

The data must therefore cover excursions relevant to the intended question. Training and validation should include appropriate disturbance directions, phases, and magnitudes, with independent cases reserved for testing. A forecast that begins at the disturbance also poses a different task from one initialized after observing part of the recovery. We distinguish these protocols explicitly below.

Record length, measurement quality, unobserved state, and contact events further constrain what can be learned. These are practical considerations in building a useful model, not reasons to abandon the modeling question. The appropriate test is whether the fitted model predicts relevant responses beyond simple reference forecasts and whether that conclusion survives independent data.

## How well do existing modeling approaches meet those needs?

We compare seven classes of model. Three are linear: Hankel-DMD, a time-invariant linear operator on histories of measurements [@brunton2017; @kutz2016]; a phase-varying linear model whose matrices are smooth (Fourier) functions of the stride phase, which we call Fourier in phase; and a phase-binned linear model with separate maps for 20 phase bins [@rosenberg2020]. Four are nonlinear: an echo state network (ESN) [@jaeger2001], a long short-term memory network (LSTM) trained as in @winner2023, a neural ODE [@chen2018], and a spectral-submanifold model (SSMLearnPy) [@haller2016; @cenedese2022]. Their flexibility, fitting procedures, and computational demands differ. The experiments assess those practical differences; they are not a proof that one model class is universally superior. We do not compare transformers [@vaswani2017]. They forecast from a finite window of past observations rather than evolving a state, so they offer no vector field, cycle, or linearization to examine, and they typically need far more data than individual gait recordings provide. They can be useful forecasters, but they are not dynamical models in the sense required here.

We test each requirement in turn, on systems whose behaviour is known (oscillators and a walking model with disturbances) and on human recordings: the 15-s walking trials and 22 long treadmill running trials of about 320 strides from four people [@maus2015], whose length allows models to be fitted with progressively more data. Predictions are evaluated by autonomous rollout: after initialization, no further observations are supplied, and forecasts are scored by the variance they leave relative to the mean-cycle reference forecast. Validation should resemble the intended use: across the benchmark's DMD and ESN tuning grids, rollout-validation errors rank settings by their test forecast error more reliably than one-step errors (median rank correlations 0.71–0.88 versus −0.19 to 0.40; @suppfig-validation). Every model's settings were chosen on its training data; where tuning effort differed, the captions say so.

### R1: Can they forecast the response?

Because walking is disturbed at every step (@fig-transient), its future contains a predictable part, the response to disturbances already received, and an unpredictable part, the responses to disturbances still to come. No model can forecast the second. We therefore first test forecasts on the kicked SLIP walker of @fig-transient A, where the predictable part is known exactly: the noise-free continuation of the true state, which sets a floor on the variance any forecast leaves (@fig-predictable). Models are trained on 60 steps (about 30 strides, comparable to two 15-s gait recordings) or 300 steps of one walk, observed with 1% measurement noise in stride-normalized time, and their settings are chosen by multistart rollout error on an independent walk. From 300 starts at random phases in ten held-out walks, each forecast is warmed up on four strides of observations and runs freely for three strides.

The predictable horizon is short. With speed feedback, the floor rises from a remaining variance of 0.27 over the first stride to 0.68 over the next two, because most of the later deviation comes from disturbances that have not yet occurred. Every model achieves most of the attainable variance reduction in the first stride: with the full centre-of-mass state and 60 training steps, from 82% for Hankel-DMD to 90–91% for SSMLearnPy and the neural ODE[[LSTM_SLIP]]. Beyond the first stride they separate. Fourier in phase and the ESN retain 62–63% of the attainable reduction, the neural ODE 46%, and Hankel-DMD and SSMLearnPy 24–27%. With 300 training steps the linear models and the ESN approach the floor (86–93%), while the neural ODE stays at 50%. Open loop, where disturbances decay more slowly and more of the future is predictable, Fourier in phase retains 97% over strides 1–3, the ESN and DMD 86%, the neural ODE 82%, and SSMLearnPy 22%. The neural ODE needed the stride phase as an input; without it, its forecasts were no better than the mean cycle even over the first stride.

Black, what happened; dashed, the noise-free continuation of the true state, which no forecast can improve on without knowing future disturbances; dotted lines, the following disturbances. (B–D) Remaining variance relative to the mean-cycle reference forecast, MSE / MSE of the mean cycle (1: no better than the mean cycle), scored against what happened, in bins of 0.1 stride, 60 training steps; medians over seeds. Black, the floor (the noise-free continuation); dotted grey, repeating the last observed step; linear models solid, nonlinear models dashed. (B) SLIP with speed feedback (ρ = 0.87 per step), full state. (C) Open loop (ρ = 0.95 per step), full state. (D) With feedback, height only. Shading, the first stride. (E) Share of the attainable variance reduction, (1 − model) / (1 − floor), over the first stride and over strides 1–3; filled, 60 training steps; open, 300.](figures/Figure_05){#fig-predictable fig-alt="One SLIP forecast with the true future and its predictable part; remaining forecast variance against horizon for six model classes, persistence and the floor under feedback, open loop and height-only observation; and the share of the attainable variance reduction for every model and condition."}

Larger disturbances are harder (@suppfig-large-kicks). After kicks of about one cycle SD to a pair of coupled FitzHugh–Nagumo oscillators, the ESN forecast the fast return of the cycle's amplitude almost exactly, whereas DMD carried a waveform error, and neither predicted the slow recovery of the coordination between the two oscillators. A model that is linear in delay coordinates approximates a cycle's phase and decaying modes well only near the cycle; far from it, part of a kick is attributed to the cycle's own harmonics and persists. Large deviations are therefore where nonlinear models are needed, and the case for linear models cannot rest on forecast accuracy alone. Earlier single-disturbance experiments with small kicks are also in the supplement (@suppfig-small-kicks).

On human data the response is a small part of the signal. Deviations from the average stride are a few percent of the joint-angle range (@fig-gait-mean), so a cycle error of a fraction of a percent, in waveform or timing, is as large as the response itself. One alternative to modeling the whole signal is to supply the cycle, as a phase and an average stride, and to model only the deviation from it. Near a stable cycle, deviations evolve linearly with a dynamics that repeats every cycle (Floquet theory), so the natural model is linear with a matrix that varies with phase, as in phase-varying models of human gait [@revzen2012; @rosenberg2020].

We compared the two approaches on the running recordings. Phase was taken from the two leading principal components of a half-stride window of all joint angles, strides were resampled to 100 samples, and the deviation was measured from a 61-stride moving-average stride (@suppfig-running-method). In their own time frames, the whole-signal models forecast the recorded joint angles closely (@fig-running A, B). With 150 training strides, the linear models, the ESN and a neural ODE erred by 7–9% of the signal's spread one eighth of a stride ahead, in real time and in stride-normalized time alike, rising to 14–17% and 10–13% at a full stride. In real time they did better than a mean-cycle template whose phase is taken from the recent history (18–21%), because they track the timing of the coming strides. In stride time, where the timing is given, the template is the average stride (11%); the two linear models matched it over a full stride, and the ESN and the neural ODE for about a quarter of a stride. SSMLearnPy, whose low-dimensional manifold carries the cycle but little of the deviation, trailed the others in both frames (12% and 11% one eighth of a stride ahead, 18% and 12% at a full stride). For the whole-signal linear model this required a weak ridge penalty and a high rank: a penalty scaled to the leading singular value, which in a whole-signal delay matrix belongs to the cycle, removes the deviation's dynamics at any rank. These errors are as large as the deviations from the average stride, which carried only 0.9% of the signal's variance: forecasting the joint angles closely does not show that a model forecasts the response.

Modeled as a deviation, the response was learnable, and Fourier in phase learned it best (@fig-running C). With 150 training strides it left 0.32 of the deviation's variance one eighth of a stride ahead. The nonlinear models given the same phase information stayed near the time-invariant linear model (0.62): the ESN left 0.55 and the neural ODE 0.60. The phase-binned model left 0.41, SSMLearnPy 0.86, and a lattice-constrained model, which imposes the cycle and a single decaying mode, at least 0.94. An LSTM trained as in @winner2023, also given the phase, forecast 6% of a stride ahead as well as the others (0.31) but drifted when run on its own predictions, leaving more variance than the average stride one eighth of a stride ahead (1.08); its training and early stopping see only one-step errors.

### R2: Do they keep walking when run on their own?

A model that forecasts the next stride may still drift, collapse, or blow up when run for longer. We ran every model freely for 30 cycles in three settings (@fig-selfdriving B): a benchmark of 13 cells (four simulated oscillators, including SLIP, with clean and with noisy training windows, and five human gait trials), the SLIP walker of R1 (8 conditions, 10 held-out walks each), and the 22 running trials (whole signal, in real and in stride-normalized time). The linear models kept the cycle almost everywhere. Fourier in phase did so in 12 of the 13 benchmark cells (it blew up on one gait trial), on all 80 SLIP walks and in all 44 running runs; Hankel-DMD in 12 of 13 cells (one decayed slowly), on all 80 walks and in 43 of 44 runs. This does not depend on DMD's spectral constraint: tuned without one, DMD also keeps the cycle in 12 of 13 cells. The nonlinear models were less dependable, and how dependable depended on the setting. In the benchmark the ESN kept the cycle in 60% of its runs, SSMLearnPy in 62% and the neural ODE in 42%[[LSTM_R2B]]; the rest collapsed, blew up, or settled on the wrong rhythm. On the SLIP walker and the running whole signal the ESN kept the cycle every time, whereas SSMLearnPy blew up in 32% and 23% of runs; the neural ODE, given the stride phase there as Fourier in phase is, kept the cycle on all 160 SLIP walks. A stricter test asks how long each free run stays close to the true cycle (@fig-selfdriving D). Within half a cycle standard deviation, about one and a half times the largest departure of the held-out data, 92% of the runs of both linear models remained for all eight stored cycles, against 58–65% for the nonlinear models. Staying on the cycle is not forecasting the response. With clean training windows, the linear models and the ESN predicted the first free-running cycle closely (relative remaining variance at most 0.26 in every cell); with noisy ones no model did much better than the mean-cycle template (medians 0.95–1.0 for Fourier in phase, DMD and the ESN; 2.3 and 5.4 for SSMLearnPy and the neural ODE; @fig-selfdriving C).

Run freely, a model of the deviation should return to the average stride, since no new disturbances arrive (@fig-selfdriving E). On the running deviations the linear models and SSMLearnPy did so within a few strides, whereas the ESN and the neural ODE settled into persistent oscillations of 0.09 and 0.22 of the deviation's SD[[LSTM_R2]]. The phase-binned model is a set of direct maps for each horizon and cannot be run freely at all. These outcomes describe the tested configurations, not intrinsic guarantees, and staying near the cycle does not establish correct perturbation dynamics.

![**Do the models keep walking when run on their own? (R2).** (A) Benchmark free runs from the end of a 12-cycle training window in the realistic regime (1% measurement noise; process noise on the simulated systems) for FitzHugh–Nagumo, coupled FHN, coupled Van der Pol, SLIP walking and one able-bodied gait trial, in z-scored units. Grey, held-out data; colour, free runs of every seed (ESN 8, LSTM 2, neural ODE 4) or polynomial degree (SSMLearnPy 2), overlaid; runs that leave the frame are cut. Labels give the outcome counts after 30 cycles. (B) Outcome after 30 free-running cycles in three settings, all runs pooled: the benchmark (13 cells: four simulated systems with 30 clean and with 12 noisy training cycles, and five gait trials); the SLIP walker of @fig-predictable (8 conditions, 30 strides from the first test start of each of 10 held-out walks; seeds pooled); and the running whole signal of @fig-running (22 trials, 150 training strides, in real and stride-normalized time; the neural ODE and LSTM were not run freely there). Ok: amplitude 0.75–1.33 of the data's and period within 10%; decays: the right period, amplitude 0.25–0.75; wrong rhythm: period off, or amplitude above 1.33; collapse: amplitude below 0.25; blow-up: non-finite or above 4. Hankel-DMD as tuned (with the spectral constraint the training data selected, usually placing persistent modes on the unit circle) and tuned by the same criterion with no constraint. (C) Benchmark: forecast error over the first free-running cycle per system (realistic and long regimes); black bars, the mean-cycle reference forecast (relative remaining variance 1); points at 10 diverged, points at 0.01 lie below it. (D) Benchmark: share of free runs remaining within ε = 0.5 cycle SD (RMS over channels) of the true cycle over the eight stored cycles: for the simulated systems, the noise-free cycle; for SLIP, its settled cycle; for gait, where no true cycle is known, the states observed in training; dotted, DMD without a constraint. The held-out data stay within 0.32 of the same references. (E) Running deviations (150 training strides): free runs of 30 strides from 40 starts per trial, the deviation's RMS at the end of each stride relative to its SD; median and interquartile range over starts and trials (seed 1); the phase-binned model's direct maps cannot run freely. Settings were chosen on the training data only (DMD, ESN and Fourier in phase: fitted on all but the last two training cycles, selected by the free-run error over those cycles and the amplitude of a longer free run); the neural ODE uses one fixed recipe, SSMLearnPy the configuration tuned on gait, and the LSTM the recipe of @winner2023.](figures/Figure_07){#fig-selfdriving fig-alt="Grid of phase portraits of free runs for six model classes on five systems; the outcome after 30 free-running cycles for each model in the benchmark, on the SLIP walker and on the running recordings; first-cycle errors with a mean-cycle reference level; the share of runs staying near the true cycle; and free runs of the running deviation models."}

### R3: Do they give reproducible answers?

Linear models fitted by ridge regression, and SSMLearnPy, have no random seed: the same data and settings give the same fit. The ESN, the LSTM and the neural ODE depend on one (@fig-reproducible). On the running deviations, forecasts one eighth of a stride ahead from ESN fits with five different reservoirs differed by 12% of the deviation's variance (median over trials), a fifth of the ESN's own error, and 6 of its 110 fits, on three trials, forecast worse than the average stride while other seeds on the same trials did not. Neural ODE fits from five initializations differed by 15%, a quarter of their own error, and none forecast worse than the average stride; but a quantity a study would compare between people (R6) varied between its seeds half as much as between trials (@fig-reproducible C)[[LSTM_R3]]. In the free-running benchmark, the seeds of the ESN and of the neural ODE ended in different fates in 9 of the 13 system–regime cells, and their first-cycle remaining variance differed between the best and worst seed by a median factor of 5.3 and 3.3. A conclusion about a person drawn from one fit of a seed-dependent model can therefore depend on the seed.

![**Reproducible answers (R3).** Models that depend on a random seed (the ESN's reservoir; the LSTM's and neural ODE's initialization and minibatches) refitted with several seeds on the same data; linear models fitted by ridge regression and SSMLearnPy have no seed, so the same data and settings give the same fit. (A) Running deviations (22 trials, 150 training strides): forecasts one eighth of a stride ahead from 5 seeds, the squared difference between seeds relative to the deviation's variance (mean over seed pairs; colour), against the model's remaining variance (median over seeds; grey); open, above 1.1. (B) The remaining variance of every trial and seed, trials ordered by their median; lines span the seeds; dashed, the average stride. (C) A quantity a study would compare between people (@fig-heterogeneity A): its spread between seeds as a share of its spread between trials. (D) The free-running benchmark of @fig-selfdriving: the first-cycle remaining variance of every seed in every system and regime (L, long; R, realistic) for the ESN (8 seeds) and the neural ODE (4 seeds).](figures/Figure_08){#fig-reproducible fig-alt="Disagreement between forecasts from different random seeds for each model on running data, per-trial remaining variance by seed, the seed share of between-trial spread of a person-level quantity, and per-cell first-cycle errors by seed in the benchmark."}

### R4: Do they work with realistic recordings?

Gait recordings are short, noisy, and partly observed (@fig-realistic). Record length matters most. On the running deviations, Fourier in phase's remaining variance one eighth of a stride ahead fell from 0.72 with 16 training strides to 0.59 with 32 and 0.32 with 150, while the time-invariant linear model levelled off after about 32 strides; the ESN and the neural ODE needed more data for the same accuracy (0.78 and 0.84 with 16 strides). Phase dependence has to be estimated economically: the phase-binned model, which divides the data among 20 phase bins, left 0.85 with 32 strides and caught up only near 64; representing the matrices as smooth functions of phase shares information across the stride. SSMLearnPy needed 150 strides to beat the average stride, and the LSTM did not at any size. A 15-s walking trial, about 9–15 strides, lies where every model is weak, which explains why no model forecast the 15-s gait trials better than the mean cycle. Added measurement noise narrowed Fourier in phase's lead: at noise equal to the deviation's own spread it matched the ESN (0.65 and 0.64), while the neural ODE (0.76) and the time-invariant model (0.80) lost more. Measurement noise also biases the multipliers of fitted return maps, as in @fig-floquet-maps. Observing only the height of the SLIP walker, Fourier in phase, the ESN and SSMLearnPy still achieved 74–77% of the attainable variance reduction over strides 1–3, whereas the neural ODE (−14%) and Hankel-DMD (−49%) left more variance than the mean cycle[[LSTM_PARTIAL]]. Choosing the settings and fitting one running trial took 1.5 s (phase-binned) to 23 s (ESN) on one CPU core, and 38 s (neural ODE) and 65 s (LSTM) per trial even when 22 trials were trained at once on a GPU.

![**Working with realistic recordings (R4).** (A) Record length: running deviations (@fig-running C), remaining variance one eighth of a stride ahead against the number of training strides; shaded, the strides in a 15-s walking trial. (B) Measurement noise: the same with added white noise in units of each channel's deviation SD, 150 training strides (the LSTM and the lattice only without noise). (C) Partial observation: SLIP with speed feedback (@fig-predictable), the share of the attainable variance reduction over strides 1–3 with the full centre-of-mass state (filled) and with height only (open), 60 training steps. (D) Cost: time to choose the settings and fit one running trial with 150 strides, on one CPU core (median over trials; SSMLearnPy timed on one trial), or for the GPU-trained models the time to train all 22 trials at once on one GPU divided by 22.](figures/Figure_09){#fig-realistic fig-alt="Remaining forecast variance of running deviations against training strides and added noise for each model class, the share of the attainable variance reduction with full and partial observation of SLIP, and the time per fit for each model class."}

### R5: Can their structure be read out?

Quantities computed from a fitted model, such as Floquet multipliers, transient growth, or how a disturbance spreads between movements, are useful only if the fit recovers the structure that produces the response. We fitted every model class to a simulated linear time-periodic system whose structure is known: three states, matrices that vary with phase through two harmonics, and per-cycle Floquet multipliers 0.86 and 0.15 (@fig-recovery). Fourier in phase recovered the phase-dependent matrices, with the harmonics that the system does not contain coming out near zero without thresholding; its error fell to 0.23 of the matrices' variation with 64 cycles and 0.15 with 128, whereas phase-binned maps needed about 1.5 to 2 times the data for the same error. The multipliers read from the fitted models were recovered by both phase-dependent linear models (distance 0.04–0.05 from the truth with 64 cycles), less well by the ESN and the neural ODE, whose closed-loop linearizations along their own orbits gave 0.18 and 0.17[[LSTM_R5]], and not at all by the time-invariant DMD (0.55) and SSMLearnPy (0.47), whose autonomous maps cannot represent dynamics that change across the cycle. Multipliers read from nonlinear models fitted to oscillators are compared with the truth in @suppfig-floquet-models.

![**Reading out structure: phase-dependent dynamics and Floquet multipliers recovered from data (R5).** A simulated linear time-periodic system with known structure: $z_{t+1} = A(\theta_t) z_t$ + noise, 3 states, 100 samples per cycle, $A(\theta) = I + B(\theta)/100$ with $B$ a Fourier series in the phase with harmonics 0–2 only (sparse blocks); true multipliers per cycle 0.86 and a complex pair of modulus 0.15. (A) Coefficients of $A(\theta) - I$ per cycle: truth, and the phase-varying linear model (Fourier in phase, fitted with 4 harmonics by one ridge regression) from 64 cycles. (B) Two entries of $A(\theta) - I$ over the cycle, 64 cycles: truth (dotted), Fourier in phase (median and interquartile range of 20 simulations), 20-bin phase-binned one-step maps (points and bars), and the time-invariant fit (line). (C) Error of $A(\theta)$, RMS over phases relative to its variation over the cycle, against cycles of data. (D) Floquet multipliers read from each model class fitted to 64 cycles: for the linear models, the eigenvalues of the product of the per-sample maps over a cycle; for the ESN, LSTM and neural ODE (given the phase), the closed-loop model linearized by finite differences over one cycle along its own orbit (the three largest); for SSMLearnPy, whose reduced map is autonomous, the linear part of the map; stars, the truth. (E) Distance of the three largest multipliers from the true ones after the best matching, against cycles of data; medians and interquartile ranges over 20 (linear) or 10 (nonlinear) simulations; the nonlinear models were fitted at 16, 64 and 128 cycles (the neural ODE, the costliest, at 16 and 64).](figures/Figure_10){#fig-recovery fig-alt="True and recovered Fourier coefficients of a phase-dependent linear system, two matrix entries over the cycle, the error of the recovered matrix against data, Floquet multipliers read from seven model classes in the complex plane, and their error against data."}

### R6: Can their quantities be compared across people?

For comparisons between people, a quantity computed from a model should differ between people more than between recordings of the same person. On the running data, the share of the current deviation's variance that each model expects to remain one eighth of a stride later did so for the linear models: between runners it accounted for 73–89% of its variance across trials (intraclass correlation 0.73 for Fourier in phase, 0.84 for the time-invariant and 0.89 for the phase-binned model). For the neural ODE, taking the median over five seeds, it was 0.69; for the ESN and SSMLearnPy it was 0.15 and 0.18[[LSTM_R6]], because their values scattered between trials of the same runner (@fig-heterogeneity A). The leading Floquet multiplier of the Fourier-in-phase model did not separate runners (intraclass correlation 0.03): with 150 strides it is estimated less precisely than the forecasts it summarizes.

Pooling recordings into one model is attractive when each recording is short, and it is how recurrent models of gait are usually trained [@winner2023]. Whether pooling helps depends on how different the recordings are relative to how variable each one is. We measured this as a heterogeneity ratio $H$: in the pool's shared delay embedding, the typical distance from the states of one recording to the nearest states of another, divided by the same distance between two halves of one recording. $H \approx 1$ means that two recordings are as alike as two halves of the same one, so pooling only adds data. Pooling paid only at low heterogeneity (@fig-heterogeneity B–D). Over 187 pools of 2–299 gait trials, a single DMD fitted to the pool forecast its own trials better than per-trial fits in 50% of pools with $H < 1.5$, and in 2% of pools above it. At high heterogeneity, small pools were nearly harmless and large pools were not: one linear operator can hold a few distinct cycles side by side, but not many. A trial left out of the pool was forecast worse than by its own fit at every heterogeneity. The two simulated cohorts, whose individuals differ slightly, lie at $H$ = 1.0 and 1.7 and gained slightly from pooling. The 299 gait trials, from 42 people at different speeds, lie at $H$ = 9.1. A group fit to all of them failed for every model class (median first-cycle remaining variance relative to the mean cycle: DMD 25, ESN 62, LSTM 16, against 1.3, 3.5 and 1.3 for per-trial fits). Recordings of human gait therefore call for per-person, and often per-condition, models whose quantities can be compared, rather than one model of everyone.

![**Comparing people: quantities from the linear models are repeatable within a person and differ between people, and one model for many recordings helps only when they are nearly alike (R6).** (A) Running (22 trials, 4 runners, 150 training strides): the share of the current deviation's variance each model expects to remain one eighth of a stride later, Σ‖ŷ(t + ⅛)‖² / Σ‖d(t)‖², one point per trial (median over seeds), coloured by runner; ICC, the share of its variance between runners (one-way intraclass correlation, runners as groups). (B–D) Heterogeneity $H$: in a pool's shared delay embedding (delays spanning one cycle, leading principal components), the median over pairs of recordings of the mean distance from the states of one to the nearest states of the other, divided by the same distance between two halves of one recording. Gait: 187 pools of the 299 trials (nearest neighbours, one participant, one speed band, random draws, participant groups and all trials); one Hankel-DMD fitted to each pool's training windows (settings chosen on held-back cycles), against each trial's own fit; first-cycle remaining variance relative to the mean-cycle reference forecast. Hexagons, the simulated SLIP and coupled-FHN cohorts (10 individuals each). (B) Remaining variance of the group fit over that of each trial's own fit, for the pool's own trials, median over the pool; below 1, the group fit forecasts better. (C) The same for a trial left out of the pool's fit. (D) Pool size against heterogeneity, median ratio in each cell; white, no such pools in the data.](figures/Figure_11){#fig-heterogeneity fig-alt="A per-trial quantity from each model of running grouped by runner with intraclass correlations; group-over-individual remaining forecast variance against a heterogeneity ratio for pools of gait trials and two simulated cohorts, for pooled and held-out trials, and a map of pool size against heterogeneity."}

### What is the overall comparison?

The requirements should be considered together (@tbl-scorecard). No model class meets all of them. The ESN forecasts the short-time response well, including from partial observations, and the nonlinear models are needed for large deviations; but the ESN's answers depend on its seed and its quantities scatter within a person. The time-invariant DMD sustains walking and is reproducible and cheap, but it cannot represent dynamics that change across the stride. A linear model with smooth phase dependence, given the cycle, came closest across the requirements tested here: it forecast the running deviations best with the least data, ran freely without drifting, recovered known structure, and gave quantities that separated people. Neither result removes the need to validate the response relevant to a particular application.

{{< include _scorecard.md >}}

## Why linear models are a strong foundation for this broader goal

“Linear” does not require the measured gait waveform to be sinusoidal or the underlying neuromechanics to be linear. A model can evolve linearly in an expanded representation, such as a history of movements, while reconstructing rich oscillatory signals. Choosing and validating that representation remains part of the modeling problem.

Most interpretable analyses of a nonlinear model also pass through a linearization. Floquet multipliers of a neural ODE or reservoir, response directions of a recurrent network, and transient growth of any fitted model are computed from Jacobians along the model's own cycle, which must first be located and is itself an estimate (@suppfig-floquet-models). A model that is linear in suitable coordinates provides these quantities directly. Linear phase-varying models have also predicted kinematic responses to ankle exoskeletons about as accurately as nonlinear phase-varying models [@rosenberg2020]. Linear models are therefore worth considering first, with nonlinear models adopted where their validated predictions are better.

### They make fitting and model checking tractable

For fixed delay coordinates, rank, and positive ridge regularization, linear regression has a unique solution and does not depend on an optimization seed. This supports repeatable comparisons and makes cross-validation and resampling practical. It does not eliminate choices about representation or establish that the data uniquely identify the physical system.

An explicit operator also makes assumptions inspectable. Spectral constraints can enforce desired sustained behavior directly, although the benchmark fits rarely needed them (@fig-selfdriving B). Measurement-noise bias can sometimes be analyzed and corrected, as in the earlier SLIP return-map comparison (@fig-floquet-maps) [@dawson2016; @hemati2017; @askham2018]. The correction depends on the instrument assumptions and can be variable in short records.

These advantages coexist with limitations. A delay model may reproduce a cycle while retaining an amplitude or waveform error, and it may fail to predict a large recovery despite relevant training examples (@suppfig-large-kicks). Its multi-stride forecasts also degrade when the state is only partly observed (@fig-predictable D). Linear models should be favored for the requirements they meet, with nonlinear alternatives retained when their validated predictions are better.

### They let us ask richer questions about the response

The companion work motivates examining non-normality and response structure beyond the spectrum [@hess2026nonnormality]. In a validated linear model, these tools address complementary questions:

- **Transient growth:** which disturbances produce the largest excursions over a specified number of strides, and when?
- **Response directions and coordination:** which combinations of movements are amplified, and where does the response appear?
- **Resolvent gains:** which temporal patterns of repeated forcing produce large responses for the specified inputs and outputs?
- **Pseudospectra:** how sensitive are spectral conclusions to changes or uncertainty in the fitted operator?

These quantities require a defined state, norm, perturbation, and observation. Amplification of a whole delay history is not automatically amplification of an instantaneous physical kick. Likewise, an undamped resolvent can be singular at a neutral mode; a model with modes placed on the unit circle needs an explicit evaluation convention. The present manuscript motivates these analyses as capabilities of linear models; it does not yet establish a new validated physical-response result from the pending resolvent experiment.

The aim is a connected description of gait response: prediction, amplification, coordination, and sensitivity considered together. Physical meaning comes from the chosen inputs and outputs and from agreement with independent responses, not simply from having a matrix to analyze.

## What does this mean for human gait studies?

Return to the questions of response and recovery. A model fitted to ordinary walking may characterize a person's usual movement pattern very well while providing little evidence about a substantial disturbance. What it establishes must be distinguished from what requires informative perturbations or changes in task.

As shown earlier, the usual gait pattern dominates the tested recordings and can dominate whole-trajectory operator measures (@fig-gait-mean).


The mean cycle also identifies individuals at least as well as the tested operator signature (@suppfig-identification). Distinguishing people is therefore not equivalent to identifying their response dynamics. In the tested 15-second recordings and out-of-trial evaluations, the examined linear models do not predict the next stride's deviation better than the mean-stride reference (@suppfig-lattice). This is a result about these data and analyses, not a universal statement that human gait is unpredictable.

Known cycle structure can be imposed on a linear model [@kvalheim2021]. The lattice-constrained SLIP example shows how that structure can help organize recovery, while the human-data comparison shows that imposing structure does not create predictive information absent from the tested recordings (@suppfig-lattice).

Models fitted during active walking describe the combined observed mechanics and control. Attributing their responses to a physiological mechanism, or separating feedback from the mechanical plant, requires additional experimental information. Applications should therefore be posed as testable questions: whether a response feature differs between people or conditions, changes with training, a device, or impairment, or predicts recovery during an independent perturbation task.

## Conclusion

The goal is to understand and predict how walking responds, compensates, and recovers. Asymptotic stability contributes to that description but is not an adequate primary target on its own. Models should be judged by their ability to predict relevant responses, sustain credible behavior, provide reproducible and interpretable estimates, work within practical recording and computational constraints, and support comparison across people and conditions.

Across these requirements, linear models offer a strong foundation for studying gait dynamics. Their value lies in the combination of tractable fitting, explicit assumptions, and tools for examining the response. That promise must be realized through appropriate experiments and independent validation, including recognition of cases where nonlinear models predict recovery better.

::: {#suppfig-large-kicks}
![](figures/Figure_S03){fig-alt="Example forecasts after an amplitude kick and a coordination kick in coupled FitzHugh-Nagumo oscillators, and forecast error and recovery over cycles for Hankel-DMD and an ESN across all held-out kicks."}

**Large kicks: fitted models forecast the fast return of the cycle's amplitude, but not the slow recovery of coordination.** Two coupled FitzHugh–Nagumo oscillators in a smooth regime ($\varepsilon = 0.25$, coupling 0.025), no measurement or process noise. Training: 24 sequences, each two undisturbed cycles and eight cycles after a kick of 0.4–1.6 cycle SD (RMS per coordinate), half along the cycle's amplitude (both oscillators displaced alike) and half against the coordination (displaced in opposite directions); settings chosen by five-cycle rollout error on eight further sequences. Both models also observe the standardized coordination signal $w_1 - w_2$; the imposed jump is excluded from DMD's and the ESN's regression targets. Test: 16 held-out kicks, four phases × two sizes (0.8, 1.3 SD) × two kinds. Forecasts start from two cycles of history ending in the kicked state and run for 12 cycles with no later observations. (A, B) One kick of each kind, 1.3 SD, chosen by the truth's excursion before any model was fitted: $v_1$ (A) and $w_1 - w_2$ (B). Dashed black, truth; blue, Hankel-DMD; orange, the ESN's four seeds. (C, D) Forecast error per cycle after the kick (RMS distance from the true state, in training SD), median and interquartile range over the 8 held-out kicks of each kind (the ESN: median over seeds first). Dotted grey, the forecast that the kick changed nothing (the unkicked continuation). (E) Coordination kicks: RMS distance to the true limit cycle per cycle, for the truth (dashed) and each model's forecast; the distance ignores timing, so it measures predicted recovery alone.
:::

::: {#suppfig-small-kicks}
![](figures/Figure_S04){fig-alt="Earlier small-perturbation recovery comparisons for coupled FHN and SLIP, and fitted SLIP multipliers."}

**Predicting the return to the true cycle from real perturbed states, and what each model's own cycle has learned (R1, R3).** Models trained on the same 10 decays × 3 cycles were warmed up on the true perturbed trajectory and run freely. Deviation = distance to the curve through the true cycle's samples, RMS over each cycle after the warm-up, for model and truth alike; median over 4 starts, kicked at 4 phases of the cycle. Black, truth; one line per fit: Hankel-DMD is one least-squares fit, the ESN 4 seeds and the neural ODE 3 seeds at fixed tuned settings. Triangles, distance of each fit's settled cycle from the true cycle, below which its deviation cannot fall. (A) Coupled FHN, per cycle: the truth returns at 0.69 per cycle, but every model's cycle is displaced from the true cycle by as much as the perturbation, so distance to the true cycle includes persistent waveform and coordination errors. (B) SLIP, centre-of-mass state (y, ẋ, ẏ), per step: the perturbation is larger than the models' cycle offsets, and every model tracks the return. (C) SLIP: multipliers of each model's own cycle, rotation against modulus per step. DMD, eigenvalues of its operator in the cycle frame (rotation from the nearest harmonic); square, the one next to the 8th harmonic; ESN, the leading eigenvalue of the monodromy of its own settled cycle (closed-loop Jacobians chained over one period, phase eigenvalue removed), one per seed; star, the exact multiplier (0.769 ∠ 13.6°); diamond, the lattice-constrained fit (@suppfig-lattice).

This earlier experiment uses a sharper FHN regime ($\varepsilon = 0.08$, coupling 0.02) and observes 170 post-perturbation samples before autonomous prediction. It is distinct from the smoother, immediate-kick experiment in @suppfig-large-kicks. Small difference signals are sensitive to timing discrepancies; the FHN result does not establish that the model classes cannot learn recovery.
:::

::: {#suppfig-running-method}
![](figures/Figure_S05){fig-alt="Six joint angles of a running trial with stride boundaries, the loop of the two leading principal components that defines the phase, strides with their average, the deviation with its state window, responses of the same deviation started at four phases, and one forecast."}

**How the phase-varying linear model of running deviations is built, on one trial** [@maus2015]. (A) Six sagittal joint angles (standardised) and the stride boundaries. (B) The phase: the two leading principal components of a half-stride window of all angles trace a loop, and the phase θ is the angle around it; a stride ends each time θ completes a turn (unlike the Hilbert phase of one joint, this does not pin any channel at the cut). (C) Every stride resampled to 100 samples; the average stride is a 61-stride moving average. (D) What is modelled: the deviation from that average stride; its state z is the last 8 samples. (E) The model, z~t+1~ = A(θ~t~) z~t~ with A(θ) a Fourier series in θ (up to 8 harmonics), fitted by one ridge regression of z~t+1~ on [z~t~, cos θ~t~·z~t~, sin θ~t~·z~t~, …]: the same knee deviation evolves differently depending on where in the stride it starts. With no harmonics the model is time-invariant DMD of the deviation. (F) One forecast from a held-out stride, with strides 1–150 fitted.
:::

::: {#suppfig-floquet-models}
![](figures/Figure_S06){fig-alt="Floquet multipliers read out of neural ODEs, ESNs and DMD against the known truth for several systems and data regimes."}

**Floquet multipliers read out of fitted models, against known truth.** For each system and data regime, the transverse multiplier is read from the model's own limit cycle by chaining one-step Jacobians over one period (neural ODE, ESN), or by a variational probe on data-delay windows (Hankel-DMD, coupled FHN only). Neural ODE, 4 seeds on one data set; ESN, 8 seeds on one data set plus one ESN per data realisation (10); DMD, 8 analysis settings (window ½ or 1 cycle × rank 16, 30, 50, 80; least squares) × 10 data realisations. Points are drawn only for runs that settled on a cycle; runs that collapsed or whose period is more than 10% off the data period are marked.
:::

::: {#suppfig-identification}
![](figures/Figure_S07){fig-alt="Identification accuracy of individuals from different gait feature families, with chance level."}

**Identifying individuals: the mean cycle does as well as the operator signature.** The companion paper's split-half protocol: each person's trials are split at random into halves, features are averaged per half and z-scored against the able-bodied half-A distribution, and a person is identified when their other half is the nearest (cosine) match among all 42 people. Mean and 95% range over 200 random splits; dashed, chance (1/42). Deviation features can carry within-stride timing jitter and marker artefacts.
:::

::: {#suppfig-lattice}
![](figures/Figure_S08){fig-alt="The lattice-constrained model on one SLIP decay, Koopman spectra of the lattice and Hankel-DMD, SLIP off-cycle metrics for all models, gait forecasts' remaining variance, remaining variance against assumed multiplier, and remaining variance under different selection rules."}

**Imposing the limit cycle's structure on a linear model.** (A) The lattice-constrained model on one SLIP decay: state = fitted cycle a(θ) plus one Floquet mode Re[ψ e^μt^ b(θ)]; the phase advances uniformly, the mode shrinks by the multiplier and turns by its rotation every step, and its shape b(θ) repeats every step. (B) A stable limit cycle's Koopman spectrum is a lattice: read relative to the nearest harmonic, every harmonic sits at (0°, 1) and every Floquet sideband at the star. Hankel-DMD (same 10 three-step decays) fits each eigenvalue on its own; the lattice fit returns one value. (C) SLIP off-cycle metrics, 4 starts: |error| of the 4-step relaxation rate (the metric of @suppfig-small-kicks, before its scoring was corrected) and distance to the true cycle after 25 steps relative to the initial distance. (D) Human gait and kicked SLIP walks: remaining variance relative to the mean stride (1 − R² of the deviation) 1 stride ahead (filled; 2 strides ahead, open) from half a stride of data; median and interquartile range over trials; multiplier and DMD rank chosen on the person's other trials. (E) Remaining variance over strides +1 and +2 against the assumed multiplier modulus: kicked SLIP walks have a minimum near the truth; gait profiles are flat at the mean stride's error. (F) The lattice model's remaining variance with the multiplier chosen out of trial (solid), on the scored strides (dashed), and on stride-shuffled copies of each trial (dotted): on gait about half of the on-test variance reduction is selection, and the rest does not carry over to other trials.
:::

::: {#suppfig-forecast}
![](figures/Figure_S09){fig-alt="Forecast error against lead time for SSMLearnPy and Hankel-DMD with mean-cycle and last-stride reference levels; per-trial errors; example knee-angle forecasts."}

**Forecasts on held-out gait against reference forecasts.** Every method gets the same information (z-scored joint angles up to sample 1000 of each 15-s trial) and is scored on the same held-out targets by the instantaneous RMSE across the six channels. (A) Median error against lead time for the tuned SSMLearnPy delay map and a rank-70 Hankel-DMD (ridge 10^−4^, stabilised; the companion paper's settings), with two reference forecasts that need no dynamics: repeating a phase-aligned mean training cycle (phase template) and repeating the last stride; interquartile range shaded for the template and the SSM. (B) Per trial at 2.7 s lead: SSMLearnPy error against the mean-cycle reference's. (C–E) Knee angle in one representative trial per group.
:::

::: {#suppfig-node-gait}
![](figures/Figure_S10){fig-alt="Hip-knee diagrams of neural-ODE forecasts for three trials, forecast error against lead time, and learned period and multiplier against training loss."}

**Neural ODEs on real gait: a good fit, an unconstrained dynamics.** A deliberately over-parameterised neural ODE (3 × 128, about 35,000 parameters against 3,000 training values), trained by multiple shooting on 10 s of six z-scored joint angles from one trial per group, six random seeds each. (A–C) Hip–knee angle–angle diagrams (limb 1): grey, training strides; black, the held-out 5 s; colour, each seed's autonomous forecast from the last training sample. (D) Forecast error against lead time for every seed, with the phase-aligned mean-cycle template for reference. (E) Period of the cycle each learned field settles onto, relative to the measured stride period, against the validation error of the autonomous forecast over the held-out 5 s. (F) Transverse Floquet multiplier of that cycle against the same validation error: held-out forecasts do not pin the dynamics.
:::

::: {#suppfig-offcycle}
![](figures/Figure_S11){fig-alt="Deviation from each model's own attractor against cycles after an off-cycle start, for DMD, ESN and neural-ODE fits and the truth."}

**Off-cycle relaxation of models trained on decays from perturbed starts.** The true system is started off its cycle; each model, warmed up on 170 samples of that trajectory, then runs freely. Deviation is the distance to the nearest point of the model's own attractor (independent of phase), RMS over each cycle, relative to the first cycle; for the truth, the distance to the true cycle, which decays by the multiplier every cycle. One line per fitted model (DMD, tuned setting; ESN and neural ODE, one line per seed), median over 4 start phases; runs that blew up are not drawn.
:::
